stem:
A 29-year-old woman has been trying to conceive for 14 months. Her periods come every 6 to 10 weeks, she has a BMI of 34 kg/m² and she has mild facial acne. Her partner's semen analysis is normal.

Which mechanism most likely explains her difficulty conceiving?

options.A: Rare or absent release of eggs from the ovaries
options.B: Blockage of both fallopian tubes by pelvic scarring
options.C: Fibroids distorting the cavity of the uterus
options.D: Antisperm antibodies within the cervical mucus
options.E: Endometriosis involving both of her ovaries

correct_answer: A. Rare or absent release of eggs from the ovaries
why_correct: Very irregular cycles in a woman who is struggling to conceive point to infrequent or absent ovulation, because eggs are released only occasionally. Ovulatory disorders are a leading cause of infertility, and initial work-up includes confirming ovulation with a mid-luteal phase progesterone and checking gonadotrophins when cycles are irregular. Source: NICE CKS, Infertility, Last revised in July 2023.
why_wrong: B. Tubal blockage usually follows pelvic infection or surgery and does not itself disturb cycle length. C. Fibroids distorting the cavity may cause heavy bleeding or miscarriage, not cycles that are weeks apart. D. Antisperm antibodies are an uncommon cause and are not suggested by irregular cycles. E. Endometriosis typically causes cyclical pain and painful sex rather than markedly irregular cycles.
pearl: Irregular or absent periods in a woman with subfertility usually mean ovulation is infrequent or not happening.
thinking: Trying to conceive for over a year  ↓  Normal semen analysis  ↓  Very irregular cycles suggest ovulatory dysfunction  ↓  Infrequent or absent ovulation
exam_trap: Choosing tubal blockage: tubal damage is a common cause overall, but nothing in this history points to it and cycles would remain regular.
takeaway: Markedly irregular cycles with subfertility suggest an ovulatory disorder.
notes: Original was a bare recall item with obviously unrelated distractors (ear, cornea, bone); built a vignette with plausible reproductive distractors. No figures are keyed (14 months and BMI are context only). CKS states ovulatory disorders are a leading cause of infertility. Distinct from live OG030 (PMOS diagnostic criteria) and PAN2375 (tubal factor). The vignette resembles PMOS but the question tests the ovulation mechanism, not the diagnosis.

stem:
A 48-year-old woman with a BMI of 39 kg/m² and long-standing infrequent ovulation has had several months of irregular, heavy vaginal bleeding. An endometrial biopsy shows atypical endometrial hyperplasia, and the gynaecologist explains that this result needs active management.

Why does this finding matter?

options.A: It shows that cervical cancer has already developed
options.B: It can progress to womb lining cancer if left untreated
options.C: It is a harmless oestrogen effect that needs no follow-up
options.D: It is the usual cause of fibroid growth within the uterus
options.E: It means that pelvic inflammatory disease is very likely

correct_answer: B. It can progress to womb lining cancer if left untreated
why_correct: Endometrial hyperplasia, especially with atypia, is a precursor of endometrial cancer and can progress to it if left untreated. It is driven by prolonged oestrogen exposure without enough progestogen, as occurs with obesity and anovulatory cycles, so management (progestogen therapy or hysterectomy) is individualised under gynaecology. Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 67, Management of Endometrial Hyperplasia, 2016.
why_wrong: A. Endometrial hyperplasia arises in the womb lining and is unrelated to the cervix. C. Atypical hyperplasia is not harmless; it needs treatment and follow-up because of malignant potential. D. Fibroid growth is a separate, oestrogen-sensitive process and hyperplasia does not cause it. E. Hyperplasia is a hormonal change, not an infective one, and does not indicate pelvic infection.
pearl: Endometrial hyperplasia, particularly atypical hyperplasia, is the recognised precursor of endometrial cancer.
thinking: Prolonged unopposed oestrogen exposure  ↓  Abnormal bleeding and biopsy shows atypical hyperplasia  ↓  Premalignant change of the endometrium  ↓  Risk of progression to endometrial cancer
exam_trap: Dismissing hyperplasia as a benign hormonal effect: without atypia the risk is lower, but it still needs assessment and treatment decisions.
takeaway: Atypical endometrial hyperplasia can progress to endometrial cancer, so it needs active management.
notes: Source asked which condition can precede endometrial cancer; reversed to a vignette asking why the biopsy finding matters (same learning point). Source key was sound. No percentages used. Live OG027 (risk factors), BX284 and DS141 (progestogen protection) test different points; no live item asks about the premalignant nature of hyperplasia. RCOG page opened states hyperplasia is the precursor of endometrial cancer and can progress if untreated; page shows last reviewed 26 February 2016. Management wording (progestogen or hysterectomy) is supported by the NHS postmenopausal bleeding page opened.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman in her first pregnancy has been taking a standard daily folic acid supplement since before she conceived. At her midwife appointment she says she has read that the baby's spine has already formed, so she wonders whether she can stop. She has no personal or family history of neural tube defects, takes no regular medication and does not have diabetes.

What advice should she be given?

options.A: Stop now, because the neural tube has already closed
options.B: Move to a higher prescribed dose until the birth
options.C: Replace it with a vitamin B12 supplement for the rest of pregnancy
options.D: Continue the standard dose until the end of the first trimester
options.E: Stop once the mid-pregnancy anomaly scan has been completed

correct_answer: D. Continue the standard dose until the end of the first trimester
why_correct: Women without added risk factors are advised to take a standard folic acid supplement before conception and through the first trimester of pregnancy to reduce the risk of neural tube defects. She should therefore continue until the end of that period rather than stop early. Higher-dose folic acid is reserved for women at increased risk. Source: NHS.uk, About folic acid; NICE CKS antenatal care confirms advice on folic acid should be given from first contact.
why_wrong: A. Although the neural tube closes early, the standard advice is to continue through the first trimester. B. A higher dose is prescribed only for women with risk factors such as a previous affected pregnancy, diabetes or certain anti-seizure medicines. C. Vitamin B12 is not a substitute for folic acid in preventing neural tube defects. E. There is no link between the anomaly scan and when to stop folic acid.
pearl: Standard-dose folic acid continues to the end of the first trimester; higher doses are for women with defined risk factors.
thinking: Pregnant, standard-risk, on folic acid  ↓  Neural tube forms early but advice still covers first trimester  ↓  No risk factors, so no higher dose  ↓  Continue standard dose to end of first trimester
exam_trap: A seems logical because closure happens early, but guidance still covers the whole first trimester.
takeaway: Continue standard-dose folic acid to the end of the first trimester unless risk factors call for more.
notes: Key is a time window in words (end of first trimester), not a number; the principle (continue, do not stop early or switch) is the point, and the numeric dose/duration is not tested. The NHS page says to take it for the first 12 weeks; CKS antenatal page (Last revised in October 2025) confirms folic acid advice from first contact but gives no dose detail. No live PLAB 1 item tests antenatal folic acid advice (HAE031 is treatment of folate deficiency anaemia).

stem:
A 29-year-old woman attends the emergency department with sudden, severe right-sided pelvic pain that began during sex the previous evening. A urine pregnancy test is negative. She is afebrile, and her pulse and blood pressure are normal. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a small volume of free pelvic fluid and a collapsed cyst on the right ovary, which has a normal size and preserved blood flow.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Ruptured functional ovarian cyst with minor bleeding
options.B: Ovarian torsion with loss of the ovarian blood supply
options.C: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy with intraperitoneal bleeding
options.E: Tubo-ovarian abscess secondary to pelvic infection

correct_answer: A. Ruptured functional ovarian cyst with minor bleeding
why_correct: Sudden unilateral pelvic pain after sex or exertion, a negative pregnancy test, free fluid and a collapsed cyst on an ovary with preserved blood flow identify a ruptured ovarian cyst. Stable patients are usually managed with analgesia and observation, with surgery reserved for ongoing bleeding or instability. Source: NHS.uk, Ovarian cyst (symptoms include sudden severe pain if a cyst splits).
why_wrong: B. Torsion causes pain with vomiting and an enlarged ovary with reduced Doppler flow, which are absent here. C. A negative pregnancy test effectively excludes an ectopic pregnancy. D. Appendicitis would give fever and migratory pain, and would not explain a collapsed ovarian cyst. E. A tubo-ovarian abscess would cause fever, raised inflammatory markers and a complex adnexal mass rather than a collapsed simple cyst.
pearl: Free fluid with a collapsed cyst after a sudden onset of pain points to rupture; check Doppler flow to avoid missing torsion.
thinking: Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain  ↓  Pregnancy test negative, so ectopic unlikely  ↓  Collapsed cyst, free fluid, normal ovary and flow  ↓  Ruptured ovarian cyst
exam_trap: B, ovarian torsion, is the dangerous mimic, but preserved Doppler flow and a normal-sized ovary argue against it.
takeaway: A collapsed cyst with free fluid and a negative pregnancy test means a ruptured ovarian cyst.
notes: Diagnosis-only item re-angled with a new vignette (post-coital onset, normal Doppler as the discriminator from torsion); no live PLAB 1 item has ruptured cyst as the answer (BX095/OG037 are torsion). Source key is sound. NHS page confirms rupture causes sudden severe pain and pain during sex; stable-patient conservative management is standard teaching (RCOG/NICE page not opened for this).

stem:
A 24-year-old woman with a history of deep vein thrombosis after a long-haul flight asks her practice nurse about long-acting contraception. The nurse suggests the implant placed under the skin of the upper arm. She asks which hormone it releases and whether it contains oestrogen.

Which statement about the hormone in the contraceptive implant most commonly used in the UK is correct?

options.A: Ethinylestradiol combined with a progestogen, released in a low continuous dose
options.B: Oestradiol alone, released slowly from the rod to suppress ovulation
options.C: Etonogestrel, a progestogen released alone, with no oestrogen component
options.D: Medroxyprogesterone acetate, released slowly from the rod under the skin
options.E: Copper ions, which act locally to prevent fertilisation at the implant site

correct_answer: C. Etonogestrel, a progestogen released alone, with no oestrogen component
why_correct: The implant widely used in the UK releases etonogestrel, a progestogen, and contains no oestrogen. This is why it is a progestogen-only method that can be considered when oestrogen is best avoided, although her history still needs a proper contraceptive assessment. Source: BNF, Etonogestrel (subdermal implant), accessed October 2026.
why_wrong: A. Combined hormonal methods contain ethinylestradiol, but the implant does not. B. No contraceptive implant releases oestradiol alone. D. Medroxyprogesterone acetate is the progestogen in the injectable, not the implant. E. Copper is the mechanism of the copper intrauterine device and is not a subdermal method.
pearl: The arm implant is a progestogen-only method (etonogestrel); the injectable is medroxyprogesterone and the coil is copper or levonorgestrel.
thinking: Implant in the upper arm  ↓  Subdermal rod releases a single hormone  ↓  Progestogen only, no oestrogen  ↓  Etonogestrel
exam_trap: A is tempting because oestrogen is the usual hormone people associate with contraception, but combined methods are a different class.
takeaway: The UK contraceptive implant releases etonogestrel, a progestogen with no oestrogen.
notes: Bare recall item rebuilt as a short vignette around the same fact (a history of VTE makes the oestrogen-free point relevant). I deliberately avoided stating a UKMEC category or duration of use (movable figures) and did not fetch FSRH; BNF page confirms etonogestrel subdermal implant. No live item tests the hormone content of the implant (BX502 tests only that it is LARC).

stem:
A 31-year-old woman with irregular cycles has a positive pregnancy test at her GP surgery. She cannot recall the date of her last period. The midwife needs a reliable estimate of gestational age so that screening and antenatal care can be planned correctly.

Which is the most appropriate way to establish how far advanced the pregnancy is?

options.B: Symphysis-fundal height measured at the booking visit
options.C: Serum progesterone concentration taken that day
options.D: Quantitative urinary hCG concentration at the surgery
options.E: Maternal weight gain compared with her pre-pregnancy weight

correct_answer: A. Ultrasound measurement of the fetus
why_correct: When the last menstrual period is unknown or cycles are irregular, gestational age is best established by ultrasound measurement of the embryo or fetus. NICE antenatal care recommends an early scan to determine gestational age, which also guides the timing of screening tests. Source: NICE NG201, Antenatal care, 2021.
why_wrong: B. Symphysis-fundal height is a later growth assessment and is not accurate for dating in early pregnancy. C. Progesterone levels vary widely and cannot give a gestational age. D. hCG concentration varies too much between women to date a pregnancy. E. Weight gain is non-specific and unrelated to gestational age.
pearl: Biochemical tests confirm pregnancy but only ultrasound measurement dates it when the last period is uncertain.
thinking: Positive test, last period unknown  ↓  Hormone levels vary between women  ↓  Biometry on ultrasound gives a reliable estimate  ↓  Ultrasound dating
exam_trap: C and D tempt because hormone levels rise in pregnancy, but they confirm pregnancy rather than date it.
takeaway: Date a pregnancy with uncertain last period by ultrasound.
notes: Re-angled with a new vignette (irregular cycles). No numeric gestation keyed; source key sound. NG201 1.2.14 states the early scan determines gestational age; CKS antenatal care (Last revised in October 2025) also describes the dating scan. No live duplicate found (searched 'dating', 'menstrual period').

stem:
A 27-year-old woman is visited by the community midwife six days after an uncomplicated vaginal birth. She feels well and has no fever. She describes red-brown vaginal loss that is lighter than in the first days, with no clots and no offensive smell. Her uterus is not tender and is getting smaller, and she is eating, drinking and passing urine normally.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Arrange same-day vaginal swabs and start empirical antibiotics for suspected endometritis
options.B: Refer her urgently for an ultrasound scan to look for retained placental tissue
options.C: Reassure her that this is normal lochia, and explain which warning signs need review
options.D: Prescribe tranexamic acid to reduce the loss and arrange review next week
options.E: Admit her to the maternity unit for assessment of secondary postpartum haemorrhage

correct_answer: C. Reassure her that this is normal lochia, and explain which warning signs need review
why_correct: Lochia is the normal vaginal discharge after birth, starting red and gradually becoming lighter and then pale over the following weeks. With no fever, offensive smell, clots, uterine tenderness or heavy bleeding, reassurance is appropriate. NICE advises explaining what bleeding to expect and to seek advice if it is sudden or very heavy, increases, contains clots or tissue, or comes with signs of infection. Source: NICE NG194, Postnatal care, 2021.
why_wrong: A. Endometritis would cause fever, tender uterus and offensive loss, none of which she has. B. Retained tissue would cause persistent or increasing bleeding and a bulky uterus. D. Tranexamic acid is not needed for expected, settling lochia. E. Secondary postpartum haemorrhage involves heavy or increasing bleeding, which is not described.
pearl: Lochia is expected after every birth; worry about bleeding that is sudden, heavy, increasing, clotty or offensive, or accompanied by fever or pain.
thinking: Postnatal day six, well, afebrile  ↓  Loss lighter, red-brown, no smell, no clots  ↓  Uterus involuting, non-tender  ↓  Normal lochia: reassure and safety-net
exam_trap: A and E over-treat normal lochia; the red flags are fever, offensive loss, tenderness, clots or heavy and increasing bleeding.
takeaway: Normal lochia settles gradually and needs reassurance plus clear warning signs.
notes: Source was a bare vocabulary question (name of postpartum discharge), tautological as a key; re-angled to a reassure-versus-investigate decision using the same learning point. Live items (OG050, DS020, PAOG032, PAQ16482, PAQ16356) all test abnormal bleeding or infection, not normal lochia. No figures keyed.

stem:
A 31-year-old teaching assistant who is 14 weeks pregnant spent an hour in a small classroom with a pupil who was sent home because of a blistering rash that the school nurse thinks is chickenpox. She cannot remember whether she had chickenpox as a child and has never been vaccinated. She feels well and has no rash herself.

What is the most appropriate first step?

options.A: Check her immune status and seek urgent specialist advice
options.B: Give a live varicella vaccine today to protect her and the baby
options.C: Reassure her that no action is needed unless a rash appears
options.D: Prescribe an oral antibiotic to prevent bacterial superinfection
options.E: Offer counselling about termination because of the exposure

correct_answer: A. Check her immune status and seek urgent specialist advice
why_correct: A pregnant woman with significant contact and no reliable history of chickenpox needs her immunity established urgently, usually with a varicella-zoster IgG test, together with prompt specialist advice. If she is non-immune she can be offered post-exposure prophylaxis, an antiviral or varicella-zoster immunoglobulin, because chickenpox in pregnancy carries risks for both mother and fetus. Source: NICE CKS, Chickenpox: Scenario: Exposure to chickenpox, Last revised in November 2023.
why_wrong: B. Live vaccines are not given in pregnancy and a vaccine would not protect her in time after exposure. C. Waiting for a rash wastes the window in which prophylaxis can be given. D. Antibiotics have no role in preventing chickenpox. E. Exposure alone is not an indication for termination, and she may well be immune.
pearl: In pregnancy, significant chickenpox contact with unclear immunity means check varicella-zoster IgG and take urgent specialist advice, not wait and see.
thinking: Significant contact with probable chickenpox  ↓  Pregnant with uncertain chickenpox history  ↓  Establish immunity with varicella-zoster IgG  ↓  Urgent specialist advice on prophylaxis if non-immune
exam_trap: C, reassurance until a rash appears, tempts because she feels well, but prophylaxis must be given early and depends on knowing her immune status.
takeaway: Check immunity and seek specialist advice promptly after significant chickenpox contact in pregnancy.
notes: Same learning point as source (establish immunity, seek prompt advice) in a new school-contact vignette with live-vaccine, reassurance, antibiotic and termination distractors. Not a duplicate of live ID018 (IgG-negative woman, key is aciclovir prophylaxis) or PAAKT180/PAQ15264 (woman with a rash). Checked: CKS says seek urgent specialist advice and IgG testing may be done in primary care if results are available within 24-48 hours; the key does not depend on that window. Source item UN3337 treated as a within-batch repeat of this one.

stem:
A 33-year-old woman has a positive home pregnancy test and her last period was about five weeks ago. She has had light brown spotting since yesterday but has no abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain or dizziness and looks well. Two years ago she had a right tubal ectopic pregnancy treated with methotrexate.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Advise her to repeat the urine pregnancy test in about a week and return if bleeding continues
options.B: Reassure her and book routine antenatal care with the community midwife
options.C: Refer her to the early pregnancy assessment service because of her ectopic history
options.D: Prescribe a single dose of methotrexate in case the pregnancy is tubal
options.E: Start progesterone pessaries to reduce the chance of miscarriage

correct_answer: C. Refer her to the early pregnancy assessment service because of her ectopic history
why_correct: A previous ectopic pregnancy is a recognised risk factor for another, so this woman should have the pregnancy located by early assessment and ultrasound rather than being managed expectantly as a low-risk woman with early bleeding would be. Early pregnancy assessment services accept self-referral from women with a previous ectopic pregnancy. About a third of ectopic pregnancies occur in women with no risk factors, so the possibility must always be considered. Source: NICE NG126, Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage: diagnosis and initial management, 2019 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Watchful waiting with a repeat test is only for women with early bleeding and no risk factors such as a previous ectopic pregnancy. B. Routine booking would leave the pregnancy location unconfirmed and a possible ectopic pregnancy undiagnosed. D. Methotrexate is given only once an ectopic pregnancy has been confirmed. E. Progesterone does not address the main concern, which is excluding an ectopic pregnancy, and is not given before the pregnancy has been located.
pearl: A previous ectopic pregnancy raises the chance of another, so a new positive test with bleeding should prompt early assessment to locate the pregnancy.
thinking: Positive test with early spotting  ↓  Previous tubal ectopic pregnancy is a risk factor  ↓  Low-risk watchful waiting does not apply  ↓  Refer to the early pregnancy assessment service
exam_trap: A, repeat the urine test and wait, tempts because she is well and has no pain, but that advice is reserved for women without risk factors such as a previous ectopic pregnancy.
takeaway: Previous ectopic pregnancy means early scan and assessment in any new pregnancy.
notes: Source item was a recall of 'previous ectopic increases recurrence risk'; re-angled to the management decision that follows from the risk factor (NG126 rec 1.4.10 limits expectant management to women without risk factors such as previous ectopic; rec 1.3.3 self-referral). The stem gives 'about five weeks' only as scenario context; the key does not depend on a gestation threshold. No live item on this point (live ectopic items PAOG005, PAOG013, PAQ928, OG040, OG043 are diagnosis or treatment).

stem:
A 44-year-old woman has had light bleeding after sex on and off for three months, with occasional spotting between periods. Her last cervical screening result was normal. On speculum examination a soft, smooth, red, finger-like growth on a narrow stalk is seen emerging from the cervical canal. The rest of the cervix looks healthy and the uterus is normal in size on bimanual examination.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A soft, smooth, red, finger-like growth arising from the endocervical canal is the typical appearance of a cervical polyp, a common benign cause of postcoital and intermenstrual bleeding. Polyps are usually removed in clinic and sent for histology. A cervix that looks consistent with cancer, which is not the case here, would need a suspected cancer pathway referral. Source: NICE NG12, Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Ectropion is a flat red area of glandular epithelium around the os, not a growth projecting from the canal. B. Nabothian cysts are smooth, pale or yellowish retention cysts on the cervical surface and do not usually bleed. C. Cervical cancer typically gives an irregular, friable or ulcerated cervix rather than a smooth stalked growth on an otherwise healthy cervix. E. A prolapsed fibroid is usually larger and broader and is accompanied by an enlarged uterus.
pearl: A smooth stalked growth from the cervical os with bleeding after sex is a cervical polyp, but any cervix that looks suspicious still needs suspected cancer pathway referral.
thinking: Bleeding after sex and between periods  ↓  Visible smooth red stalked growth from the os  ↓  Rest of the cervix and uterus look normal  ↓  Cervical polyp
exam_trap: A, cervical ectropion, also causes bleeding after sex and tempts, but it is a flat red area on the cervical surface rather than a growth projecting from the canal.
takeaway: A smooth, soft, stalked growth from the os is a cervical polyp, a benign cause of postcoital bleeding.
notes: Source stem was a one-line recall item; built a speculum-finding vignette with ectropion, Nabothian cyst, cancer and prolapsed fibroid as distractors. Key checked against standard gynaecology teaching: no NHS/CKS page for cervical polyps was reachable (nhs.uk, patient.info, nhsinform URLs returned 404 or no content), so NICE NG12 rec 1.5.16 was opened only to support the point that a cancer-looking cervix needs suspected cancer pathway referral. Reviewer may wish to add an RCOG or BSCCP source. No live cervical polyp item found in the bank (live OG025, DF092, PAOG065, PAQ921 cover other postcoital bleeding points).
